planting.note: Propagate by leaf or offset cuttings callused for a few days before rooting in fast-draining succulent mix; give strong light to develop the thick powdery farina and prevent stretching.

directions: A large patented hybrid rosette with broad, wavy-edged leaves coated in a heavy chalky farina that reads silvery-lilac to pale pink depending on light and season. The undulating, almost ruffled leaf margins set it apart from smoother-leaved echeverias like 'Perle von Nurnberg', and the bloom rubs off if handled, so it is best displayed rather than passed around. Branched stalks of orange, bell-shaped flowers rise above the rosette in warmer months. Give it bright, direct sun and gritty, fast-draining soil, watering deeply only once the mix is fully dry, since both shade and soggy roots dull the color and loosen the rosette form.

planting.note: Break off short stem sections and let them callus a few days before rooting in gritty succulent mix; stems root readily at any leaf node.

directions: A 1962 Myron Kimnach hybrid of Crassula rupestris subsp. marnieriana and C. perforata subsp. kougaensis, with plump, rounded, minty-green leaves stacked tightly along slender stems like beads on a string, each leaf edged in red that deepens under bright light and stress. Stems start upright then arch and trail as they lengthen, making it well suited to a hanging pot or the edge of a mixed succulent bowl, distinct from the more angular, triangular-leaved species form of C. rupestris. Small white flower clusters top the stems in late spring. Grow in bright light with some protection from the harshest midday sun, and let the soil dry fully between waterings to keep the stacked leaves plump and tight.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring or summer in lean, gritty succulent mix; allow cut ends to callus for several days before inserting to prevent rot.

directions: Long sold in the trade as Crassula 'Blue Bird', this South African subspecies of silver dollar jade is distinguished from the plain species by leaves with rippled, undulating margins in powdery blue-gray, flushing pink to fuchsia at the edges under sun and drought stress. It grows slowly into a stout, branching shrublet with a thickened trunk, eventually reaching several feet, and can be trained as a bonsai-style specimen much like Crassula ovata. Clusters of white to pale pink star-shaped flowers appear from spring into summer on established plants. Grow in full sun to bright light in fast-draining gritty soil, watering deeply and infrequently, since overwatering is the most common cause of loss.

planting.note: Take stem cuttings and let them callus for a few days before rooting in fast-draining succulent mix; brittle stems break easily and root readily from broken sections.

directions: A Chihuahuan Desert species with thick, pale blue-green leaves clustered along procumbent to pendulous stems, the older leaves often tipped in yellow or blushed pink toward the tip in strong light. It has a shrubbier, more upright-to-trailing habit than the flatter mat of Sedum clavatum, and unusually for the genus its bright yellow, star-shaped late-winter flowers carry a noticeable sweet fragrance. Well suited to a hanging basket or the front of a succulent trough where the fragrant flowers can be appreciated up close. Grow in full sun with fast-draining, mineral-heavy soil, watering only every few weeks during active growth and even less in winter dormancy.

planting.note: Lay detached leaves or stem cuttings on top of dry succulent mix to callus; leaves detach easily and root readily on their own without burying.

directions: A variegated sport of the popular jelly bean plant, with plump, cylindrical leaves streaked in pink, cream, and green instead of the solid green-to-red coloring of the standard form, and the pink and cream tones intensify with brighter light and cooler temperatures. Sprawling stems root wherever they touch soil, making it a fast, low groundcover or trailing accent for a mixed succulent bowl. Leaves detach at the slightest touch, which is a normal and effective means of propagation rather than a sign of distress. Grow in full sun in lean, fast-draining soil and allow the mix to dry completely between waterings, since excess moisture causes stretching and leaf drop.
